extracted.intended_audience: state and tribal title IV-E agencies, child welfare administrators, attorneys representing children/parents/tribes, and policy analysts preparing or implementing title IV-E claims
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance (NPRM) on when and how title IV-E agencies may claim Federal Financial Participation (FFP) for administrative costs of independent legal representation for eligible children, parents, relative caregivers, and tribal intervenors, including permitted activities, limits, and the assumptions and analyses supporting cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health care power of attorney / proxy representation (transition plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney providing independent legal representation to an eligible child to prepare for and participate in a proceeding to establish a health care power of attorney, health care proxy, or other similar document recognized under State law when it is necessary to meet the requirement to develop a transition plan in the 90-day period immediately prior to the date on which the child will age out of foster care, per section 475(5)(H) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of an allowable administrative cost claim when the representation is necessary to meet the statutory transition-plan requirement. The citation to section 475(5)(H) indicates the statutory hook for claiming FFP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation to resolve youth credit report inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney providing independent legal representation to an eligible child/parent/relative caregiver to prepare for and participate in a proceeding to resolve inaccuracies in a youth's credit report when it is necessary to meet the plan requirement to provide a youth a copy of any consumer report each year until the child is discharged from care, and provide assistance (including, when feasible, from any court-appointed advocate for the child) in interpreting and resolving any inaccuracies in the report, per section 475(5)(I) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowable where the activity is necessary to satisfy the title IV-E plan requirement to provide consumer reports and assist in resolving inaccuracies; applies to child, parent, or relative caregiver representation when needed for plan compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation to obtain/change/correct official documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney providing independent legal representation to an eligible child/parent/relative caregiver to prepare for and participate in a proceeding to help a child obtain, change, or correct official documentation when it is necessary to meet the plan requirements to provide youth discharged from foster care an official or certified copy of the United States birth certificate of the child, a social security card issued by the Commissioner of Social Security, health insurance information, a copy of the child's medical records, and a driver's license or identification card issued by a State in accordance with the requirements of section 202 of the REAL ID Act of 2005, and any official documentation necessary to prove that the child was previously in foster care per sections 475(5)(I) and 471(a)(27) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies specific documentation-related proceedings for which representation may be an allowable administrative cost when necessary to meet statutory plan requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation to access benefits/housing/education for youth aging out
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney providing independent legal representation to an eligible child/parent/relative caregiver to prepare for and participate in a proceeding to help a youth aging out of foster care access public benefits, housing, health insurance, and education when it is necessary to meet the plan requirement to develop a transition plan 90-days immediately prior to the date on which the child will age out of foster care, per section 475(5)(H) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FFP-claimable legal assistance may include civil matters that secure supports needed for successful transition out of foster care when they are necessary to fulfill the transition-plan requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable FFP for tribal attorney representation when tribe intervenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A title IV-E agency with placement and care responsibility for an Indian child may claim FFP for administrative costs of legal representation provided by an attorney representing an Indian child's tribe when the child's tribe intervenes in any state court proceeding for the foster care placement or termination of parental rights of an Indian child who is in title IV-E foster care or an Indian child who is a candidate for title IV-E foster care when such legal representation is found necessary by the Secretary to carry out the requirements in the title IV-E agency's title IV-E state plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authorizes claiming FFP for tribal intervenor representation when the Secretary finds it necessary to implement the agency's title IV-E plan requirements; includes statutory context (ICWA) and links the allowable cost to plan fulfillment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribal attorney role in conveying cultural/social standards for court determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The information provided by the tribe's attorney provides the cultural and social standards of the child's tribe that are necessary for the court to make essential determinations that reasonable efforts were made as required under the title IV-E plan; tribal attorney's representation of the cultural and social standards for family connection, reunification and what permanency looks like in the child's tribe may be necessary to finalize the permanency plan for an Indian child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of tribal attorneys is justified where their input is necessary for courts to determine reasonable efforts and permanency consistent with tribal customs (e.g., customary adoption), and to avoid unintended adverse consequences such as loss of tribal membership or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optionality of claiming FFP (agency discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: As with all allowable administrative costs, it is the option of the title IV-E agency with placement and care responsibility of the child whether or not to implement this option to claim FFP for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule establishes an optional reimbursement mechanism; it does not mandate that title IV-E agencies provide these services or claim FFP for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening of 'preparation for and participation in civil legal proceedings' activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal broadens 'preparation for and participation in civil legal proceedings' to include facilitating, arranging, brokering, advocating, or otherwise linking clients with providers and services as identified in the child's case plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted activities go beyond courtroom representation to include outreach and linkage activities when they are connected to case-plan needs and thus necessary for title IV-E plan administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible populations for independent legal representation FFP claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent legal representation provided by attorneys representing children who are candidates for title IV-E foster care, children who are in title IV-E foster care, and the children's parent(s) and relative caregiver(s) in all stages of foster care legal proceedings and certain civil legal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal extends eligibility beyond children and parents in foster-care proceedings (as reflected in prior CWPM policy) to include relative caregivers and selected civil legal proceedings necessary to meet plan requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: FFP reimbursement rate and non-Federal match requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IV-E agencies may claim reimbursement for 50 percent of the administrative costs to provide legal representation in foster care proceedings and civil proceedings, and the title IV-E agency must pay its share with state or tribal funds. This non-Federal share will be an equal percentage of 50 percent because a title IV-E agency must match the same amount of funds for which it seeks Federal reimbursement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any claimed costs should be budgeted with the understanding of a 50/50 Federal/non-Federal split; agencies must secure matching funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness and cost allocation plan requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to the Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for HHS Awards, title IV-E agencies must ensure costs are reasonable (45 CFR 75.404 applied via 45 CFR 1335.30(i)). A cost is reasonable if, in its nature and amount, it does not exceed that which would be incurred by a prudent person under the circumstances. The title IV-E agency must describe how the administrative costs of allowable legal representation are allocated in a public assistance cost allocation plan that is reviewed and approved by HHS (45 CFR 1355.30(k) applying 45 CFR 95.507).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must conform to Federal cost principles: demonstrate reasonableness and document allocation methodology in an approved cost allocation plan to substantiate title IV-E administrative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory review requirement — E.O. 12866 and 13563 cost-benefit assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity). Section 3(f) of E.O. 12866 (as modified) defines a 'significant regulatory action' including thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must perform regulatory impact analysis quantifying costs and benefits, consider distributive impacts and equity, and determine whether the action meets significance thresholds described in the Executive Orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternatives and rationale for chosen approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives considered included codifying only the existing CWPM policy (which would not allow claiming costs in non-foster care civil legal proceedings and would not allow representation for relative caregivers) and narrowly defining attorney activities. The proposal rejects those alternatives because broader civil legal representation and inclusion of relative caregivers better meet goals of prevention, reunification, and permanency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory choice must be justified by showing narrower alternatives would fail to achieve statutory or policy goals (e.g., preventing foster-care entry, expediting permanency); documentation of that rationale is part of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) small-entity impact certification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary certifies, under 5 U.S.C. 605(b), that this rulemaking will not result in a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities because it is applicable only to state and tribal title IV-E agencies; therefore, an initial regulatory flexibility analysis is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must assess whether a rule affects small entities and prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis if required; here the rule is certified not to require one because small-entity criteria are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202 of UMRA requires agencies to assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year above the statutory threshold (approximately $165 million in 2022 dollars). This rulemaking does not contain mandates that will impose spending costs on state, local, or tribal governments, or on the private sector, in excess of the threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must evaluate whether a rule imposes unfunded mandates and perform the required analysis if thresholds are crossed; the NPRM documents UMRA applicability and concludes thresholds are not exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act (CRA) 'major rule' criteria and determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRA defines a 'major rule' as one that has resulted, or is likely to result in, (1) an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more; (2) a major increase in costs or prices; or (3) significant adverse effects on competition, employment, etc. Based on estimates, OIRA anticipates that a final rule would be 'major' under the CRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulewriters must compare estimated impacts to CRA thresholds and classify the rule accordingly for notice to Congress; a 'major' designation triggers additional procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection requirements for title IV-E foster care administrative costs are currently authorized under OMB number 0970-0510 and include administrative costs for independent legal representation. This action does not include any new information collection requirements or changes to existing information collection requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rule adds or changes paperwork burdens, PRA clearance is required; the NPRM documents that no new PRA burden is introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal cost-estimation methodology and baseline assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: ACF used FY2021 title IV-E foster care administrative cost claims as the base year amounts, defining 'candidates' and 'IV-E FC' populations. Assumptions include an overall annual 1 percent caseload growth rate; FFP claims growth factors of 4.7% for FY2023 and 2.3% thereafter; separate implementation-level measures for foster care representation and tribal representation (baseline 0% for tribes, projected 5% in FY2023 and 35% in FY2027); civil proceeding implementation levels derived from the proportion of children receiving foster-care representation (20% in FY2023 rising to 56% in FY2032); and rounding conventions for published charts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost estimates rely on explicit base-year data, growth-rate assumptions, and implementation-level projections; users should treat estimates as contingent on these assumptions and adjust if local data or uptake rates differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Detroit Model to estimate civil legal representation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: For civil legal proceedings cost estimates, the NPRM uses the 'Detroit Model' legal services program data: average yearly gross cost $2,524 per client, yielding a title IV-E Federal share estimate of $1,262 (50% FFP). This was used because there were no current Form CB-496 title IV-E administrative cost claims for civil proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no direct administrative-claim data exist, agencies may rely on known program models for unit-cost estimation, but must disclose limitations and the fact that the Detroit Model was the only available program model for pre-petition civil representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget-line calculation conventions for federal cost tables
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM describes line-by-line calculations for federal costs: e.g., line 1 = national number of children receiving representation; line 2 = national average FFP claim per child; line 3 = average FFP claims for populations; line 4 = total Federal costs (line1 x line2); line 5 = non-Federal costs (equal to Federal at 50% FFP); line 6 = total Federal and non-Federal costs (sum of lines 4 and 5); and similar breakdowns for civil proceedings and tribal representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and reviewers should follow the same transparent, line-item methodology (population x unit cost = total; apply matching rate) when reproducing or scrutinizing the estimates.
